sectionGuide.why: “Reliability” alone is too vague for benchmarks or enterprise SLAs. This section names the sub-dimensions — consistency, robustness, calibration, safety — so coverage analysis and protocol design can be granular instead of a single pass/fail label.
sectionGuide.wgUse: Dimension definitions for coverage matrices, protocol families, and enterprise SLAs — use these names instead of generic “reliable”. Review before citing dimension names in failure vocabulary or metrics.
sectionGuide.enables: Metrics such as repeated-run success rate and calibration error quantify these families; failure vocabulary maps which dimension broke; coverage matrices use this decomposition when rating benchmarks.
sectionGuide.priorities: **P0** holds the Princeton-aligned families and outcome consistency — required for any reliability claim. **P2** (cross-agent agreement) is MAS-specific refinement. There is no P1 band here; review P0 before metrics and before deep failure work that cites dimension names.

categories.relevance: Decomposes vague 'reliable' into consistency, robustness, calibration, safety — required for SLAs and benchmark coverage matrices.
categories.wgUse: Coverage matrix columns · protocol families · running-notes coverage rows

terms.definition: The degree to which stated confidence or expressed uncertainty matches how often the system is actually correct. A well-calibrated system that says it is 80% confident should be right about 80% of the time in that class of cases.
terms.scopeNote: Primarily a model-level property; architecture can expose but not fully fix miscalibration.
terms.literatureNote: Well established for models (ECE in HELM, LM-Polygraph). Agent-level calibration benchmarks are early and heterogeneous (2025–2026 preprints).

terms.definition: Stability of correct outcomes when the same task is evaluated repeatedly under equivalent conditions. Unqualified use means outcome consistency across repeated runs.
terms.scopeNote: Differs from robustness: stable wrong answers are consistent but not robust to paraphrase.
terms.literatureNote: Divergent: default AAIF/princeton sense = same correct outcome on every repeat. Wojciech (running notes): Princeton HAL distinguishes outcome, trajectory, and resource consistency — see child terms. BFT 'consistency' = valid agreement (may be wrong) — use 'cross-agent agreement' with qualifier only.
academicTerms: pass@k (single-run best-of-k — not an AAIF term)

terms.definition: Within a multi-agent system, agents do not hold conflicting values for the same fact or entity at the same point in a task. A spatial property across agents, not repeated-run variance.
terms.scopeNote: Not the default meaning of consistency. Differs from cross-agent agreement, which does not require correctness.
terms.literatureNote: AAIF-specific: mutual factual consistency plus correctness requirement. Distinct from agreement and from single-agent repeat consistency.

terms.definition: Whether semantically equivalent instructions produce the same reliable outcome — for example, "cancel my subscription" and "end my plan".
terms.scopeNote: Important for enterprise deployments with varied user phrasing and locales.
terms.literatureNote: Sub-dimensions under agent reliability. Princeton HAL is the primary academic anchor; see bibliography in x-sources where listed.

terms.definition: Whether the system remains acceptably correct when tools fail, data is missing, messages are delayed, or other runtime faults occur within scope.
terms.scopeNote: Closely related to recoverability and graceful degradation.
terms.literatureNote: Sub-dimensions under agent reliability. Princeton HAL is the primary academic anchor; see bibliography in x-sources where listed.

terms.definition: Whether repeated runs on the same task produce the same success or failure result. Default meaning of unqualified consistency.
terms.scopeNote: Measured with repeated trials and repeated-run success rate.
terms.literatureNote: Aligns with tau-bench pass^k and Princeton outcome-consistency sub-dimension. Preferred plain name; 'pass^k' appears only in academicTerms and gap analysis evidence.

terms.definition: Low variation in latency, token use, API cost, and duration across repeated identical requests.
terms.scopeNote: Requires explicit qualifier. Same correct answer with wildly varying cost is a resource consistency failure.
terms.literatureNote: Thin benchmark coverage; Rabanser et al. (2026) define C_res from coefficient of variation across repeats. AAIF treats cost/latency variance as a first-class reliability concern.

terms.definition: Stability of correct outcomes when inputs are rephrased, conditions shift, or faults are injected within the evaluation envelope.
terms.scopeNote: Covers both wording changes and operational perturbations; name the perturbation type when reporting results.
terms.literatureNote: Broad term in ML (prompt robustness, adversarial robustness). AAIF splits into input paraphrase vs operational fault robustness for measurement clarity.

terms.definition: The degree to which a system avoids prohibited, harmful, or unauthorised actions under the task and control policies in force. Measured by violation rate, not by general answer correctness.
terms.scopeNote: Boundary with Security & Privacy WG for adversarial and abuse cases. A system can be reliable yet unsafe if it consistently violates policy.
terms.literatureNote: Divergent: Princeton HAL = policy/harm violation rate. Lamport/BFT 'safety' = no bad state — not the default AAIF meaning. Coordinate with Security & Privacy WG on adversarial cases.

terms.definition: Whether repeated runs follow similar action paths — tool choices, message order, and step structure — not only similar final answers.
terms.scopeNote: Requires explicit qualifier. Independent from outcome consistency.
terms.literatureNote: Emerging in agent reliability studies; rarely scored in mainstream harnesses (WebArena, SWE-bench score end-state only). Named in Rabanser et al. (2026) sub-dimension analysis.
academicTerms: path stability (When Agents Disagree With Themselves, 2026)

terms.definition: Agents converge on the same stated value or decision, regardless of whether that value is correct. Used only when explicitly discussing distributed consensus literature.
terms.scopeNote: Requires explicit qualifier; not the default meaning of consistency.
terms.literatureNote: BFT/consensus sense — agents converge to the same value, not necessarily the correct one. P2 refinement; do not confuse with outcome consistency or factual alignment.
